strengths: The paper presents an original, useful construction: generate a virtual correspondence from point coordinates and reuse established five-point and P3P solvers for the difficult four-point, three-view problem. The mean-point variant is particularly attractive because it requires neither training nor additional image features.

The experiments support competitiveness with the specialized homotopy-continuation solver. In Table 1, the learned variant improves AUC@5 from 43.25 to 47.14 on Sacre Coeur and from 19.45 to 21.34 on St. Peters’ Square. The much simpler mean-point variant achieves broadly comparable accuracy to homotopy continuation.

The evidence includes noise experiments, 10,000 real image triplets, and a supplementary two-view experiment on 9,900 image pairs. Training exclusively on synthetic data followed by successful real-image evaluation is encouraging. Table 3 also demonstrates a useful preliminary tradeoff: the mean-point two-view method achieves AUC@5 of 61.48 versus 63.71 for five-point estimation, with reported runtime decreasing from 0.04 to 0.03 seconds.

The manuscript clearly acknowledges the approximation and distinguishes the overconstrained four-triplet configuration from genuinely minimal configurations. Its evaluation of the conventional 5pt+P3P baseline, including the finding that dedicated four-point methods offer limited practical gains, is valuable. Together, the simple construction and comparative findings support weak acceptance despite the absence of an overall benchmark advantage.
weaknesses: The practical efficiency advantage is limited. Table 1 generally favors conventional 5pt+P3P in accuracy, while the learned method is substantially slower: 38.50 versus 2.59 seconds on Sacre Coeur and 14.13 versus 2.46 seconds on St. Peters’ Square. The mean-point method also takes slightly longer than homotopy continuation on both scenes. These results support simplicity and competitive four-point estimation more strongly than superior accuracy or speed.

The evaluation does not assess the complete three-camera pose. Section 5 scores rotation and translation-direction errors for pairs 1–2 and 1–3, and its RANSAC residual uses the same two essential matrices. Neither quantity measures the relative scale of the two baselines, which is observable in a calibrated three-view reconstruction. An incorrect relative baseline scale can therefore go undetected; no corresponding camera-center, reconstruction, or pair 2–3 evaluation is provided.

The conditions under which virtual correspondences remain reliable are insufficiently characterized. Figure 2 demonstrates favorable average epipolar error, while Figure 3 shows substantial pose errors even without measurement noise. The two-scene real-data evaluation does not isolate strong perspective effects or outlier rates. Consequently, the proposed advantage under heavy outlier contamination and the broader applicability claims remain preliminary.

Reproducibility of the central accuracy/runtime comparison is incomplete. Although the supplement describes the network, loss, data generation, and optimizer, the manuscript omits important RANSAC settings, including inlier thresholds, stopping budgets, and local refinement details. Handling multiple five-point and P3P solutions is also insufficiently specified.

A smaller technical clarification concerns permutation invariance: the Set Transformer backbone is invariant, but selecting the first three correspondences for the virtual point and the first two for normalization makes the complete preprocessing procedure order-dependent. Section 3.2 should qualify its invariance claim.
